plan.topic_summary: Mixture of Experts (MoE) is a sparse model architecture that routes inputs to a subset of specialized sub-networks, enabling large parameter counts with lower per-token compute. It matters for a 1-5 year view because it is reshaping the cost-performance frontier of frontier AI models and could redefine how inference and training economics scale.
key_questions: What is the current state of MoE architectures in production deployments, and how do their inference costs compare to dense models of equivalent quality?
What are the primary technical bottlenecks (memory, communication, training stability) that limit MoE scaling, and are there emerging solutions?
How is the open-source vs closed-model landscape evolving around MoE architectures over the next 1-3 years?
What are the expected cost trajectories for MoE-based inference at scale over 3-5 years, and how do they compare to alternatives like quantized dense models or hybrid architectures?
What safety and evaluation challenges are specific to MoE architectures (e.g., expert interpretability, routing opacity), and how are they being addressed?

gaps: Market evidence is thin: only one small company filing (Maase Inc.) provides verified commercial deployment data; the wave of MoE model releases (X1) is strong social signal but not backed by verified revenue or production metrics
No verified evidence on production cost comparisons between MoE and alternative scaling strategies (quantization, distillation) in real serving environments
On-device MoE claims (X4: Huawei Kirin, ModelBest on iPhone) are unverified social signals with no peer-reviewed or filing-backed confirmation

sources.title: A Survey on Mixture of Experts in Large Language Models
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have garnered unprecedented advancements across diverse fields, ranging from natural language processing to computer vision and beyond. The prowess of LLMs is underpinned by their substantial model size, extensive and diverse datasets, and the vast computational power harnessed during training, all of which contribute to the emergent abilities of LLMs (e.g., in-context learning) that are not present in small models. Within this context, the mixture of experts (MoE) has emerged as an effective method for substantially scaling up model capacity with minimal computation overhead, gaining significant attention from academia and industry. Despite its growing prevalence, there lacks a systematic and comprehensive review of the literature on MoE. This survey seeks to bridge that gap, serving as an essential resource for researchers delving into the intricacies of MoE. We first briefly introduce the structure of the MoE layer, followed by proposing a new taxonomy of MoE. Next, we overview the core designs for various MoE models including both algorithmic and systemic aspects, alongside collections of available open-source implementations, hyperparameter configurations and empirical evaluations. Furthermore, we delineate the multifaceted applications of MoE in practice, and outline some potential directions for future research.

sources.title: Not All Experts are Equal: Efficient Expert Pruning and Skipping for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
sources.abstract: A pivotal advancement in the progress of large language models (LLMs) is the emergence of the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs. Compared to traditional LLMs, MoE LLMs can achieve higher performance with fewer parameters, but it is still hard to deploy them due to their immense parameter sizes. Different from previous weight pruning methods that rely on specifically designed hardware, this paper mainly aims to enhance the deployment efficiency of MoE LLMs by introducing plug-and-play expert-level sparsification techniques. Specifically, we propose, for the first time to our best knowledge, post-training approaches for task-agnostic and task-specific expert pruning and skipping of MoE LLMs, tailored to improve deployment efficiency while maintaining model performance across a wide range of tasks. Extensive experiments show that our proposed methods can simultaneously reduce model sizes and increase the inference speed, while maintaining satisfactory performance. Data and code will be available at https://github.com/Lucky-Lance/Expert_Sparsity.

sources.title: OLMoE: Open Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
sources.abstract: We introduce OLMoE, a fully open, state-of-the-art language model leveraging sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE). OLMoE-1B-7B has 7 billion (B) parameters but uses only 1B per input token. We pretrain it on 5 trillion tokens and further adapt it to create OLMoE-1B-7B-Instruct. Our models outperform all available models with similar active parameters, even surpassing larger ones like Llama2-13B-Chat and DeepSeekMoE-16B. We present various experiments on MoE training, analyze routing in our model showing high specialization, and open-source all aspects of our work: model weights, training data, code, and logs.

sources.title: ExpertFlow: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Inference via Predictive Expert Caching and Token Scheduling
sources.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can outperform dense large language models at similar computation by activating only a small set of experts per token. However, stacking many expert modules introduces substantial parameter memory, which makes MoE models difficult to deploy in memory-constrained environments such as single-GPU devices. Offloading alleviates this issue by storing inactive experts in CPU memory and loading them on demand, but existing methods remain limited: static caches disregard input-dependent routing, and methods that train separate models to predict expert usage ahead of time are often inaccurate or require significant training cost. We propose ExpertFlow, a lightweight MoE inference system that addresses this routing dependency through three coordinated components: 1) a transformer-based routing path predictor that estimates expert usage across all MoE layers in a single forward pass, 2) a token scheduler that groups tokens with similar predicted routes to improve expert utilization, and 3) a predictive expert cache that loads only the required experts while correcting mispredictions at runtime. Together, these components enable efficient expert loading and execution, reducing GPU memory usage by up to 93.72% and improving inference throughput by up to 10x over strong offloading baselines on a single GPU.

sources.title: Convergence Rates for Softmax Gating Mixture of Experts
sources.abstract: Mixture of experts (MoE) has recently emerged as an effective framework to advance the efficiency and scalability of machine learning models by softly dividing complex tasks among multiple specialized sub-models termed experts. Central to the success of MoE is an adaptive softmax gating mechanism which takes responsibility for determining the relevance of each expert to a given input and then dynamically assigning experts their respective weights. Despite its widespread use in practice, a comprehensive study on the effects of the softmax gating on the MoE has been lacking in the literature. To bridge this gap in this paper, we perform a convergence analysis of parameter estimation and expert estimation under the MoE equipped with the standard softmax gating or its variants, including a dense-to-sparse gating and a hierarchical softmax gating, respectively. Furthermore, our theories also provide useful insights into the design of sample-efficient expert structures. In particular, we demonstrate that it requires polynomially many data points to estimate experts satisfying our proposed \emph{strong identifiability} condition, namely a commonly used two-layer feed-forward network. In stark contrast, estimating linear experts, which violate the strong identifiability condition, necessitates exponentially many data points as a result of intrinsic parameter interactions expressed in the language of partial differential equations. All the theoretical results are substantiated with a rigorous guarantee.

sources.title: MoE-LLaVA: Mixture of Experts for Large Vision-Language Models
sources.abstract: Recently, remarkable progress has been made in scaling up Large Language Models (LLMs) through the use of the sparse Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) layers without significantly increasing computational cost. However, the transition from a pre-trained LLM to a sparse Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) with MoE remains an open challenge. Directly fine-tuning an LLM to a sparse LVLM often leads to training collapse, characterized by (1) a large modality feature distribution gap and (2) expert load imbalance. This paper proposes a three-stage decoupled weight training process. In the first two stages, the model learns to adapt the LLM to an LVLM. In the third stage, the FFN weights from the second stage are used as lossless initialization for expert weights, effectively constructing a sparse model with a vast number of parameters while maintaining constant computational cost. Through extensive ablation experiments, we derive three empirical guidelines and propose a sparse LVLM termedMoE-LLaVA. MoE-LLaVA is a MoE-based sparse LVLM architecture, which uniquely activates only the top-$k$experts through routers during deployment, keeping the remaining experts inactive. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MoE-LLaVA outperforms LLaVA-1.5-7B with an average improvement of 4.6 across nine visual understanding benchmarks. Notably, with only 2.2B active parameters, our MoE-LLaVA shows comparable result with LLaVA-1.5-13B (87.0 vs. 85.9) on POPE benchmark. Our work establishes a baseline for sparse LVLMs and provides empirical guidelines for exploring the sparse LVLMs. Our code is available at:https://github.com/PKU-YuanGroup/MoE-LLaVA.

sources.title: Mixture-of-Experts Models in Vision: Routing, Optimization, and Generalization
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable conditional computation by routing inputs to multiple expert subnetworks and are often motivated as a mechanism for scaling large language models. In this project, we instead study MoE behavior in an image classification setting, focusing on predictive performance, expert utilization, and generalization. We compare dense, SoftMoE, and SparseMoE classifier heads on the CIFAR10 dataset under comparable model capacity. Both MoE variants achieve slightly higher validation accuracy than the dense baseline while maintaining balanced expert utilization through regularization, avoiding expert collapse. To analyze generalization, we compute Hessian-based sharpness metrics at convergence, including the largest eigenvalue and trace of the loss Hessian, evaluated on both training and test data. We find that SoftMoE exhibits higher sharpness by these metrics, while Dense and SparseMoE lie in a similar curvature regime, despite all models achieving comparable generalization performance. Complementary loss surface perturbation analyses reveal qualitative differences in non-local behavior under finite parameter perturbations between dense and MoE models, which help contextualize curvature-based measurements without directly explaining validation accuracy. We further evaluate empirical inference efficiency and show that naively implemented conditional routing does not yield inference speedups on modern hardware at this scale, highlighting the gap between theoretical and realized efficiency in sparse MoE models.

sources.title: DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model
sources.abstract: We present DeepSeek-V2, a strong Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model characterized by economical training and efficient inference. It comprises 236B total parameters, of which 21B are activated for each token, and supports a context length of 128K tokens. DeepSeek-V2 adopts innovative architectures including Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and DeepSeekMoE. MLA guarantees efficient inference through significantly compressing the Key-Value (KV) cache into a latent vector, while DeepSeekMoE enables training strong models at an economical cost through sparse computation. Compared with DeepSeek 67B, DeepSeek-V2 achieves significantly stronger performance, and meanwhile saves 42.5% of training costs, reduces the KV cache by 93.3%, and boosts the maximum generation throughput to 5.76 times. We pretrain DeepSeek-V2 on a high-quality and multi-source corpus consisting of 8.1T tokens, and further perform Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) to fully unlock its potential. Evaluation results show that, even with only 21B activated parameters, DeepSeek-V2 and its chat versions still achieve top-tier performance among open-source models.

sources.title: Task-Conditioned Routing Signatures in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Transformers
sources.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable efficient scaling of large language models through conditional computation, yet the routing mechanisms responsible for expert selection remain poorly understood. In this work, we introduce routing signatures, a vector representation summarizing expert activation patterns across layers for a given prompt, and use them to study whether MoE routing exhibits task-conditioned structure. Using OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct as an empirical testbed, we show that prompts from the same task category induce highly similar routing signatures, while prompts from different categories exhibit substantially lower similarity. Within-category routing similarity (0.8435 +/- 0.0879) significantly exceeds across-category similarity (0.6225 +/- 0.1687), corresponding to Cohen's d = 1.44. A logistic regression classifier trained solely on routing signatures achieves 92.5% +/- 6.1% cross-validated accuracy on four-way task classification. To ensure statistical validity, we introduce permutation and load-balancing baselines and show that the observed separation is not explained by sparsity or balancing constraints alone. We further analyze layer-wise signal strength and low-dimensional projections of routing signatures, finding that task structure becomes increasingly apparent in deeper layers. These results suggest that routing in sparse transformers is not merely a balancing mechanism, but a measurable task-sensitive component of conditional computation. We release MOE-XRAY, a lightweight toolkit for routing telemetry and analysis.

sources.title: Scaling Laws for Fine-Grained Mixture of Experts
sources.abstract: Mixture of Experts (MoE) models have emerged as a primary solution for reducing the computational cost of Large Language Models. In this work, we analyze their scaling properties, incorporating an expanded range of variables. Specifically, we introduce a new hyperparameter, granularity, whose adjustment enables precise control over the size of the experts. Building on this, we establish scaling laws for fine-grained MoE, taking into account the number of training tokens, model size, and granularity. Leveraging these laws, we derive the optimal training configuration for a given computational budget. Our findings not only show that MoE models consistently outperform dense Transformers but also highlight that the efficiency gap between dense and MoE models widens as we scale up the model size and training budget. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the common practice of setting the size of experts in MoE to mirror the feed-forward layer is not optimal at almost any computational budget.

sources.title: GEM: Graph-Enhanced Mixture-of-Experts with ReAct Agents for Dialogue State Tracking
sources.abstract: Dialogue State Tracking (DST) requires precise extraction of structured information from multi-domain conversations, a task where Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle despite their impressive general capabilities. We present GEM (Graph-Enhanced Mixture-of-Experts), a novel framework that combines language models and graph-structured dialogue understanding with ReAct agent-based reasoning for superior DST performance. Our approach dynamically routes between specialized experts: a Graph Neural Network that captures dialogue structure and turn-level dependencies, and a finetuned T5-Small encoder-decoder for sequence modeling, coordinated by an intelligent router. For complex value generation tasks, we integrate ReAct agents that perform structured reasoning over dialogue context. On MultiWOZ 2.2, GEM achieves 65.19% Joint Goal Accuracy, substantially outperforming end-to-end LLM approaches (best: 38.43%) and surpassing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods including TOATOD (63.79%), D3ST (58.70%), and Diable (56.48%). Our graph-enhanced mixture-of-experts architecture with ReAct integration demonstrates that combining structured dialogue representation with dynamic expert routing and agent-based reasoning provides a powerful paradigm for dialogue state tracking, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency through selective expert activation.

sources.title: Lifecycle Mixture of Experts: Staggered Death Prevents Expert Collapse in Mutual Activation MoE
sources.abstract: Abstract re of Experts (MoE) architectures su er from expert collapse, where experts converge to homogeneous representations during training, nullifying the bene ts of conditional computation. We study the mutual activation MoE a router-free architecture where experts activate each other through sigmoid-gated cross-connections and show that collapse is inevitable under standard training (mean pairwise cosine similarity > 0.93). We propose Lifecycle MoE, a mechanism that detects collapse via similarity and cross-activation metrics, then kills and rebirths experts to restore di erentiation. Our key nding is that staggered death killing only one expert at a time with a cooldown period preserves system stability while breaking collapse, achieving T2 accuracy within 0.5pp of baseline (vs. 48pp degradation with simultaneous death). Extended 120-epoch training reveals a self-stabilization property: only a single death event is needed to permanently prevent re-collapse, with consensus accuracy reaching 62.57% (vs. 49.19% baseline, a +13.4pp gain). We further show that snapshot-based revival and similarity-targeted death are redundant or counterproductive, while Linear-capacity experts naturally resist collapse. These results establish staggered lifecycle as a simple, e ective, and self-limiting mechanism for maintaining expert diversity in mutual activation MoE.

sources.title: MoEless: Efficient MoE LLM Serving with Serverless Experts
sources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures to scale efficiently under stringent resource constraints. However, MoE's sparse activation causes severe expert load imbalance, where a few experts become stragglers while others remain underutilized, leading to inflated inference latency and cost. Existing solutions assume static, serverful model deployments, limiting expert elasticity and often incurring costly expert swapping or degraded output quality. We present MoEless, an efficient serverless MoE serving framework that mitigates expert load imbalance via elastic expert execution. MoEless leverages lightweight, layer-aware predictors to estimate incoming expert load distributions and proactively identify stragglers. We design optimized scaling and placement strategies to improve function locality, GPU utilization, and cross-expert load balance. MoEless is prototyped on top of Megatron-LM and deployed on an eight-GPU testbed. Experiments with open-source MoE models and real-world workloads show that MoEless reduces inference latency by 43% and inference cost by 84% compared to state-of-the-art solutions.

sources.title: Preventing Expert Collapse in MoE-dVLMs via Modality-Wise Norm Alignment
Scaling Multi-Node Mixture-of-Experts Inference Using Expert Activation Patterns
sources.abstract: Most recent state-of-the-art (SOTA) large language models (LLMs) use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures to scale model capacity without proportional per-token compute, enabling higher-quality outputs at manageable serving costs. However, MoE inference at scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by expert load imbalance and inefficient token routing, especially in multi-node deployments where tokens are not guaranteed to be routed to local experts, resulting in significant inter-node all-to-all communication overhead. To systematically characterize these challenges, we profile SOTA open-source MoE models, including Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek V3-671B, and Qwen3-230B-A22B, on various datasets and collected over 100k real expert activation traces. Upon studying the expert activation patterns, we uncover various persistent properties across all the frontier MoE models: variable expert load imbalance, domain-specific expert activation where expert popularity shifts across task families (code, math, chat, general), and a strong correlation between prefill and decode expert activations. Motivated by these findings, we propose workload-aware micro-batch grouping and an expert placement strategy to maximize token locality to the destination expert, thereby reducing inter-node communication. Across models and datasets, these optimizations help reduce all2all communication data up to 20, resulting in lower MoE decode latency and better accelerator utilization.

sources.title: Experts Are Decoding Interfaces, Not Knowledge Containers: A 0:167 Asymmetry in MoE Collapse Experiments
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: This paper originates from a speculative philosophical thought — the Information-Dimension Cyclic Model — which posits, as a groundless fantasy about physical reality, that: (1) information is a substrate more fundamental than matter or energy, (2) dimensions are display frameworks through which information manifests at varying resolution, and (3) every minimum information unit contains seeds toward higher dimensions. Under this view, matter and time are merely emergent after-effects of information spontaneously constructing dimensions; dimensions continually arise, collapse, and are reborn in a cyclic manner. **These three axioms are not testable claims about the physical world, nor do they correspond to any linguistic or computational domain. They are offered as pure imaginative speculation.** The experiments described in this paper do not attempt to verify these axioms. Rather, they constitute a free conceptual projection — we borrow the metaphor of "dimensional collapse and holographic residue" and map it, without logical necessity, onto the architecture of Mixture-of-Experts Transformers. This is an associative thought experiment, not a causal test. Projecting this imagery onto a small MoE Transformer trained on structured narratives, we simulate "dimensional collapse" by destroying experts, then measure recovery dynamics. A battery of six experiments reveals: (1) a 4.95x cross-recovery advantage after collapse, indicating information redundancy in the shared infrastructure; (2) a 0:167 asymmetry between the contribution of surviving experts and shared infrastructure to recovery speed; (3) a counterexample (G2) where preserving the "best expert" while reinitializing shared components *worsens* performance below random initialization, ruling out the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis as a competing explanation; (4) SVD analysis showing destroyed experts lose all subspace structure while shared components remain intact; (5) single-token probing showing that holographic projection at the individual token level is not supported — rather, information distribution exists at the interaction topology level; and (6) a dual-channel architecture experiment showing a modest 1.15x cross-recovery boost from explicitly preserving global embedding fingerprints. The concrete findings — that in MoE architectures, information resides in shared infrastructure rather than individual experts, and that experts function as parallel decoding interfaces rather than independent knowledge containers — stand independently of the philosophical framing. All experiments are reproducible on CPU.

sources.title: FLEX-MoE: Federated Mixture-of-Experts with Load-balanced Expert Assignment for Edge Computing
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enable scalable neural networks through conditional computation, offering enhanced effectiveness and efficiency for next-generation wireless communications. However, deploying MoE with federated learning (FL) over wireless and IoT edge networks faces two critical challenges: 1) resource-constrained clients cannot store large AI models with full expert sets, and 2) non-IID data distributions cause severe expert load imbalance that degrades model performance. To this end, we propose FLEX-MoE, a federated MoE framework that jointly optimizes expert assignment and load balancing under limited client capacity. Specifically, our approach introduces client-expert fitness scores that quantify expert suitability for local datasets through training feedback, and employs an optimization-based algorithm to maximize client-expert specialization while enforcing balanced expert utilization system-wide. Unlike greedy methods that focus solely on personalization while ignoring load imbalance, FLEX-MoE addresses expert utilization skew, which is particularly severe in heterogeneous edge FL. Our experimental results demonstrate superior accuracy and consistently balanced expert utilization across diverse resource-constrained scenarios for edge computing.

sources.title: MoE-LLaVA: Mixture of Experts for Large Vision-Language Models
sources.abstract: Recently, remarkable progress has been made in scaling up Large Language Models (LLMs) through the use of the sparse Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) layers without significantly increasing computational cost. However, the transition from a pre-trained LLM to a sparse Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) with MoE remains an open challenge. Directly fine-tuning an LLM to a sparse LVLM often leads to training collapse, characterized by (1) a large modality feature distribution gap and (2) expert load imbalance. This paper proposes a three-stage decoupled weight training process. In the first two stages, the model learns to adapt the LLM to an LVLM. In the third stage, the FFN weights from the second stage are used as lossless initialization for expert weights, effectively constructing a sparse model with a vast number of parameters while maintaining constant computational cost. Through extensive ablation experiments, we derive three empirical guidelines and propose a sparse LVLM termedMoE-LLaVA. MoE-LLaVA is a MoE-based sparse LVLM architecture, which uniquely activates only the top-$k$experts through routers during deployment, keeping the remaining experts inactive. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MoE-LLaVA outperforms LLaVA-1.5-7B with an average improvement of 4.6 across nine visual understanding benchmarks. Notably, with only 2.2B active parameters, our MoE-LLaVA shows comparable result with LLaVA-1.5-13B (87.0 vs. 85.9) on POPE benchmark. Our work establishes a baseline for sparse LVLMs and provides empirical guidelines for exploring the sparse LVLMs. Our code is available at:https://github.com/PKU-YuanGroup/MoE-LLaVA.

sources.title: BaGuaLu-2: Taming Dynamic Memory Fluctuation for Efficient MoE Model Training over 10,000 GPUs
sources.abstract: Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is the de facto architecture for scaling large language models. However, dynamic expert load imbalance causes severe memory fluctuations that degrade training efficiency. Existing systems rely on static memory provisioning: they either over-provision, leaving GPU memory idle during normal execution, or under- provision, inviting out-of-memory crashes and costly manual rollbacks when load spikes occur. To address these challenges, we propose BaGuaLu-2, a large-scale MoE training system that eliminates this dilemma through flexible provisioning. By transforming memory allocation from a static, one-time tuning choice into a continuous and fine-grained control. BaGuaLu-2 grants exact activation memory on demand for each training batch. Furthermore, it offsets any dynamic management overhead through system optimizations. BaGuaLu-2 demonstrates exceptional scalability, training a model with 1040 billion parameters across 12,288 GPUs while sustaining over 2 EFlops at 35% MFU. Compared with state-of-the-art systems, BaGuaLu-2 delivers 1.14x and 1.13x average throughput improvements over Megatron-Kuai and AdaPipe, respectively.

sources.title: Less is MoE: Trimming Experts in Domain-Specialist Language Models
sources.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models achieve strong performance through conditional computation, but their large parameter footprint poses deployment challenges.Prior MoE compression approaches catastrophically fail when evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks beyond commonsense reasoning.We trace this failure to the granularity of compression: important capabilities are distributed across experts but concentrated in FFN sparse intermediate dimensions.To identify these dimensions, we use Fisher importance which outperforms activation-, router-score-, and magnitude-based alternatives, and identifies tiny sets of taskcritical dimensions: in Qwen1.5-MoE,removing as few as 12 of 2.03M routed-FFN intermediate dimensions collapses GSM8K accuracy while largely preserving factual-knowledge performance.Building on this, we propose Fisher-MoE, which operates within FFN to remove intermediate dimensions ranked by Fisher importance.At the same 50% MoE compression ratio, Fisher-MoE preserves model capability, while reducing weight memory by ∼45% and improving inference throughput by 21%.These findings suggest intermediate dimension granularity is an effective unit for both compression and ranking where capability concentrates in MoE models.Our implementation is available in an anonymous repository.

sources.title: MoA: Heterogeneous Mixture of Adapters for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
sources.abstract: Recent studies integrate Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) to further enhance the performance of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods in Large Language Model (LLM) applications. Existing methods employ \emph{homogeneous} MoE-LoRA architectures composed of LoRA experts with either similar or identical structures and capacities. However, these approaches often suffer from representation collapse and expert load imbalance, which negatively impact the potential of LLMs. To address these challenges, we propose a \emph{heterogeneous} \textbf{Mixture-of-Adapters (MoA)} approach. This method dynamically integrates PEFT adapter experts with diverse structures, leveraging their complementary representational capabilities to foster expert specialization, thereby enhancing the effective transfer of pre-trained knowledge to downstream tasks. MoA supports two variants: \textbf{(i)} \textit{Soft MoA} achieves fine-grained integration by performing a weighted fusion of all expert outputs; \textbf{(ii)} \textit{Sparse MoA} activates adapter experts sparsely based on their contribution, achieving this with negligible performance degradation. Experimental results demonstrate that heterogeneous MoA outperforms homogeneous MoE-LoRA methods in both performance and parameter efficiency. Our project is available at https://github.com/DCDmllm/MoA.

sources.title: GaP-MoE : Explicit Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts via Orthogonal Gradient Accumulation and Projection
sources.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) models improve scalability by routing input tokens to only a subset of expert networks, but they often suffer from representation collapse, in which multiple experts converge toward similar functions and lose their intended diversity. Prior work has addressed this limitation either by improving router architectures or by introducing auxiliary loss terms that implicitly penalize similarity among experts. However, router-based approaches remain vulnerable to routing collapses, and loss-based approaches can conflict with the task's original objective during optimization. In this work, we propose GaP-MoE (Gradient Accumulation and Projection in MoE), which induces expert specialization by directly manipulating expert output gradients rather than modifying the loss function. At each training step, GaP-MoE stochastically selects one of the $TopK$ routed experts as a leader based on normalized routing scores, and projects the gradients of the remaining follower experts onto the orthogonal complement of the subspace spanned by the leader's recent gradients. This removes directional overlap between expert gradients without altering the task loss, allowing specialization to emerge as a direct consequence of the optimization dynamics rather than an externally imposed constraint. We evaluate GaP-MoE in both fine-tuning settings (BERT-based, on GLUE) and from-scratch pretraining settings (GPT-2-based, on WikiText-103, enwik8, and text8), and further confirm its compatibility as a drop-in module for existing SMoE architectures. Experimental results show that GaP-MoE achieves performance comparable to or better than standard SMoE.

sources.title: Harnessing Routing Foresight for Micro-step-level MoE load balancing in RL Post-training
sources.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) and reinforcement learning (RL) post-training now dominate large language model (LLM) development, yet expert load imbalance remains a critical challenge. Existing load-balancing systems target pre-training by relying on historical step-level statistics. However, these methods fail under the unique workload dynamics of RL post-training: the step-level load is stable, but the tiny batch sizes processed during micro-steps cause severe, high-frequency load fluctuations. We introduce ForeMoE, a micro-step-level load balancing system for MoE RL post-training. Instead of relying on historical statistics, ForeMoE exploits the multi-stage RL pipeline (rollout, recompute, policy update) by using foreseeable routing information from the rollout stage to proactively guide load balancing in the remaining stages. To support frequent per-micro-step reconfiguration, ForeMoE employs a hierarchical planner that decomposes the NP-hard load balancing problem into tractable sub-components, alongside a transfer engine that leverages complementary hardware paths (CPU-assisted and GPU-direct) for overlapped expert transfer. Evaluations on 64 GPUs demonstrate that ForeMoE achieves up to a 1.45$\times$ speedup over state-of-the-art RL post-training systems.

findings.claim: Expert load imbalance shows up as a recurring bottleneck across MoE training, multi-node inference, serverless serving, RL post-training and federated settings. Each paper proposes its own fix, which suggests the problem is unresolved rather than solved.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Five independent abstracts, four of them arXiv preprints that are not peer reviewed, describe imbalance as severe or critical in different regimes. Interpretation: the number of separate mitigations suggests no general fix exists yet. The abstracts do not compare the fixes with one another.
findings.supporting_excerpt: MoE inference at scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by expert load imbalance and inefficient token routing

findings.claim: Multi-node MoE inference carries a communication cost because tokens are not guaranteed to be routed to local experts. This leads to heavy inter-node all-to-all traffic. Expert popularity also shifts by task domain, so a static placement may not stay efficient.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: A single arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. It is based on profiling open-source models, and the reported reduction ('up to 20') has lost its unit in the abstract text. The headline gain therefore cannot be interpreted precisely. Actual cost on proprietary production traffic is a gap.
findings.supporting_excerpt: resulting in significant inter-node all-to-all communication overhead

findings.claim: Expert or representation collapse, where experts converge to similar functions and negate the value of conditional computation, is repeatedly reported. Proposed fixes differ widely (gradient projection, heterogeneous adapters, kill-and-rebirth, norm alignment), and none appears to be established as standard.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Several preprints agree collapse is a problem. Lifecycle MoE reports pairwise cosine similarity above 0.93 in a non-standard router-free architecture, so it may not transfer to mainstream top-k sparse MoE. The GaP-MoE abstract is truncated, and its tests (BERT/GLUE, GPT-2-scale) are small relative to frontier models. src_fddf5596ed has only a title and no abstract, so it is weak support. None of these results is peer reviewed except possibly the conference item, and that one has no abstract.
findings.supporting_excerpt: they often suffer from representation collapse, in which multiple experts converge toward similar functions and lose their intended diversity.

findings.claim: Converting a pre-trained dense LLM into a sparse MoE vision-language model can fail outright. The cited failure is training collapse, driven by a modality distribution gap and expert load imbalance. Success needed a bespoke multi-stage training recipe.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The MoE-LLaVA abstract states the failure mode and a three-stage workaround. The results are on small models (2.2B active parameters), so scaling behaviour is not shown. The title of src_fddf5596ed also points to expert collapse in multimodal MoE, but there is no abstract to confirm.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Directly fine-tuning an LLM to a sparse LVLM often leads to training collapse

findings.claim: MoE total parameter footprint is a deployment burden, and compressing it is fragile. Prior compression methods are reported to fail badly on general benchmarks, and removing a tiny number of FFN dimensions can wipe out math ability (GSM8K) while leaving factual recall largely intact. This points to hidden, concentrated capability and a risk of silent degradation.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: One EMNLP-type paper, one abstract. The sensitivity result is shown on Qwen1.5-MoE only, so generality is unknown. The proposed Fisher-MoE (45% memory reduction, 21% throughput gain) is the authors' own fix and is not independently reproduced here.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Prior MoE compression approaches catastrophically fail when evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks beyond commonsense reasoning.

findings.claim: At very large scale, MoE training efficiency is limited by dynamic memory fluctuation, with a risk of out-of-memory crashes and manual rollbacks. Even a flagship 12,288-GPU run sustains only 35% MFU, and the gain over competing systems is modest (about 1.13-1.14x).
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Interpretation of one arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed). The abstract states 35% MFU and 1.14x/1.13x improvements, and describes crashes under static provisioning. The inference that substantial hardware capacity remains unused is mine. The experiment depends on a very large bespoke cluster, so independent reproduction is unlikely and this is a gap rather than a proven flaw.
findings.supporting_excerpt: sustaining over 2 EFlops at 35% MFU

findings.claim: Reported serving and post-training speedups come from narrow, author-run setups and are measured against chosen baselines. The examples are a prototype on an eight-GPU testbed (43% latency and 84% cost reduction) and a 64-GPU evaluation (up to 1.45x). These figures may not carry over to production fleets.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Both are arXiv preprints, not peer reviewed. Baselines are described only as 'state-of-the-art'. The abstracts give no variance, workload diversity or hardware-diversity evidence. MoEless also relies on predictors of expert load, which could degrade when workload patterns shift, though the abstract does not test this.

findings.claim: Edge and federated deployment of MoE is constrained because clients cannot hold full expert sets, and non-IID data aggravates expert utilization skew. This limits MoE's practicality outside datacenters without added assignment and balancing machinery.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: A single arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. The abstract claims 'superior accuracy' without numbers, and shows no real-device or real-wireless validation. This is a gap in evidence, not proof of failure.
findings.supporting_excerpt: resource-constrained clients cannot store large AI models with full expert sets, and

hype_flags: 'Scale efficiently / without proportional compute': this covers per-token FLOPs only. Memory footprint, all-to-all communication, load imbalance and utilization costs all appear in these papers.
'MoE is the de facto architecture' (src_dd9539f5eb): this is a framing in an arXiv abstract, not a measured result, and says nothing about whether alternatives could displace it.

'Experts are decoding interfaces, not knowledge containers' (src_6bd8a3b4a4): the paper calls its own work speculative, an associative thought experiment and not a causal test, on a small MoE trained on narratives. It should not be treated as evidence about expert function.
Large percentage gains (84% cost, 43% latency, 'up to 20' communication reduction): these come from self-run comparisons on small or unspecified testbeds, and one figure lost its unit.

'Self-stabilizing' collapse prevention in Lifecycle MoE: this rests on a router-free toy-scale setting (62.57% accuracy) from a non-peer-reviewed Research Square preprint, and may not apply to production sparse MoE.

finding.claim: S1 and S2 treat MoE's decoupling of parameters from compute as general. It holds for per-token FLOPs only. Total parameters must still be stored, moved and communicated, so 'minimal extra computation' does not mean minimal extra memory, bandwidth or serving complexity.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The ExpertFlow abstract itself states the memory cost. The multi-node inference abstract adds inter-node all-to-all traffic. The findings cite the 236B/21B and 7B/1B ratios without this caveat, which makes the compute saving look like an overall cost saving.
finding.supporting_excerpt: stacking many expert modules introduces substantial parameter memory, which makes MoE models difficult to deploy in memory-constrained environments such as single-GPU devices.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S3 credits MoE sparsity together with MLA for the cost savings, but the abstract does not separate their contributions. The 93.3% KV-cache reduction comes from MLA, which is not an MoE feature. The 42.5% training-cost and 5.76x throughput figures are developer-reported against a different model (DeepSeek 67B), and the abstract gives no ablation. These numbers cannot be read as the benefit of MoE.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract says 'MLA guarantees efficient inference through significantly compressing the Key-Value (KV) cache' and that DeepSeekMoE enables economical training. It does not say how much each component contributes, and DeepSeek 67B may differ in data and recipe. This is a single-developer preprint, and only the abstract was reviewed.

finding.claim: S4 presents the scaling-law result as a general 'MoE beats dense' conclusion. The efficiency gap is defined in terms of training compute budget and fitted laws. It does not cover wall-clock speed, memory, communication or serving cost, and the widening gap is an extrapolation from fitted laws, not a measurement at frontier scale. The source is a single preprint with only the abstract available.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract frames its results around 'computational budget' and optimal training configuration. The small vision study (src_e65e8a2f49) reports that naive conditional routing gave no inference speedup at its scale. This suggests FLOP-based advantages do not automatically become practical advantages, so the conclusion needs a scope caveat.

finding.claim: S6 says expert pruning and skipping preserves performance across tasks, and the abstract does not support that strength. It claims only 'satisfactory performance'. Other evidence reports that MoE compression can fail badly on general benchmarks and can silently remove concentrated capabilities such as math.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The Not All Experts abstract says 'maintaining satisfactory performance' and gives no numbers. The Less is MoE paper reports that removing as few as 12 of 2.03M intermediate dimensions collapses GSM8K accuracy. Whether it is referring to the S6 method specifically cannot be told from the abstracts, but the 'preserving performance' wording is too strong without caveats.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Prior MoE compression approaches catastrophically fail when evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks beyond commonsense reasoning.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S10 sets a CIFAR10 classifier-head study against systems papers as if they were contradictory evidence on wall-clock speedup. They are not comparable. The vision study tests naive routing in a small classifier head. ExpertFlow's 10x is measured against other offloading baselines, not against dense inference or in-memory MoE. The result is therefore 'different questions', not 'mixed evidence'.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The vision result is explicitly scale-limited ('at this scale'). The ExpertFlow gains are 'up to' best-case figures 'over strong offloading baselines on a single GPU'. Neither abstract tests whether MoE is faster than a dense model at equal quality, which is the question the finding implies it addresses.
finding.supporting_excerpt: naively implemented conditional routing does not yield inference speedups on modern hardware at this scale
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S11 uses GEM as evidence of MoE applied beyond LLM pretraining and quotes its 65.19% vs 38.43% accuracy, which is misleading. GEM's 'experts' are a GNN and a T5-Small model combined with ReAct agents. This is not a sparse, learned-expert MoE like the LLM systems in the rest of the set. The gain cannot be attributed to MoE. The comparator ('best end-to-end LLM approach cited') is unspecified, and the source is a single preprint.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: GEM is a pipeline with a router between two heterogeneous models plus agent reasoning. The reported improvement bundles graph structure, fine-tuning and ReAct, so it says little about MoE as such. The 38.43% LLM baseline may also be a weak or non-comparable one.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Our approach dynamically routes between specialized experts: a Graph Neural Network that captures dialogue structure and turn-level dependencies, and a finetuned T5-Small encoder-decoder for sequence modeling
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S7 generalises from one small model (OLMoE-1B-7B-Instruct) and a four-way task classification to 'MoE routing is not just a load-balancing mechanism'. Only one preprint supports it, and the abstract does not rule out lexical or format confounds. It does not test frontier-scale or other MoE designs.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract states 'Using OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct as an empirical testbed' and reports four-way classification with 92.5% accuracy. It adds permutation and load-balancing baselines but no controls for surface token statistics. The direction is plausible, and src_9ea34fdea9 reports domain-dependent expert popularity in larger models, so the problem is the breadth of the claim, not its direction.

finding.claim: S9 presents the exponential-vs-polynomial sample-complexity result without noting that it is a statistical-theory result for a specific parametric regression setting. It is not evidence about practical LLM MoE training. The 'linear experts' case is not a design in common LLM use, so its practical relevance is limited.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract frames the result as parameter and expert estimation convergence under softmax gating. It says the theory is 'substantiated with a' (truncated) set of experiments and does not claim LLM-scale validation. The finding's wording could be read as practical guidance. The abstract is truncated and this is an arXiv preprint.

finding.claim: S12 claims 'little cross-citation visible in the abstracts', which the evidence cannot support. Abstracts do not list citations, so cross-citation cannot be observed from them. The 'three separate conversations' split also looks like an artefact of which papers were retrieved. Load imbalance and expert collapse recur across training, inference, serving, federated learning and theory-adjacent work.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Several abstracts from different 'conversations' share the same load-imbalance problem, which suggests the topics are connected. The finding is already marked low confidence, but its central observable (cross-citation) is not available in abstract-only data.
finding.supporting_excerpt: MoE's sparse activation causes severe expert load imbalance, where a few experts become stragglers while others remain underutilized

finding.claim: The Science findings are almost entirely about efficiency gains and omit the recurring failure modes in the evidence set. These include expert load imbalance, expert or representation collapse, brittle compression, and cross-node communication overhead. Each paper proposes its own fix and none is shown to be standard, so the overall picture is too favourable.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The retrieved abstracts describe load imbalance as inflating inference latency and cost (MoEless), representation collapse where 'multiple experts converge toward similar functions' (GaP-MoE), and heavy all-to-all traffic (multi-node inference). Several fixes are from author-run preprints with small testbeds, so the problems may not be solved. This is a gap in coverage and does not make any single finding false.

limitations: Only 12 papers and abstracts (one has metadata only), so no full-paper methods, baselines or ablations were checked.
Most evidence is arXiv or Zenodo/Research Square preprints that are not peer reviewed; several have zero citations.
Some abstracts are truncated or garbled (src_b8a4505926, src_6bd8a3b4a4, src_9ea34fdea9 lost a unit), which limits what can be stated.

Search coverage skews toward systems and collapse papers. There is little on MoE security, safety, quality-versus-dense comparisons, hardware supply constraints or competing architectures (dense, state-space), so absence of these risks here is a gap, not evidence of safety.
Papers are mostly small-scale academic setups; evidence on frontier proprietary deployments is unavailable.
No company-level evidence was provided, so no company-specific risks are asserted.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were available. Some abstracts are truncated and one cited paper (src_fddf5596ed) has no abstract.
Most evidence is arXiv or Research Square preprints that are not peer reviewed. Several are recent and have no citation counts, so I could not check external replication.
I did not independently verify any reported numbers, and I could not check whether a compression paper's 'prior approaches' include the S6 method.
I left S5 and S8 unchallenged. Their claims match the abstracts, and the caveats about best-case speedups and bespoke training recipes are already covered by R4 and R7.
The set of 23 papers is a limited retrieval sample, so absence of contradicting evidence here does not show the findings hold broadly.

Nvidia, Toyota, Alibaba and Microsoft were flagged as patent assignees for MoE-related patents, but no patent text, filing excerpt, or headline about their MoE activities was retrieved; nothing can be said about their commercial MoE products, customers, or investment from this evidence.

market.coverage_note: Companies are chosen from the evidence: SEC-listed patent assignees and employers of paper authors found by the Patent and Science agents (25 company name(s) in the patents and papers; 4 matched to the SEC ticker file; the top 4 by patents + papers are read), plus filers whose reports mention the topic. Company evidence is limited to short verbatim passages from their latest SEC annual/quarterly reports that mention the keywords. 8-K press releases (exhibit files) are not read, and companies that do not file with the SEC (e.g. SK hynix, Samsung) are not covered. News items are headlines only: the articles were not read. Company size and trend figures (revenue, growth, R&D, net income) come from the SEC's XBRL company-facts data as reported by each company; the size class is by revenue, not market value. Companies marked 'discovered' were found by a full-text search of all SEC filings for the topic phrase only; no patent or paper of theirs was found, they are often small, and a mention in a filing says nothing about their size, role or prospects.

findings.claim: Multiple accounts report a wave of large MoE model releases and open-weights drops in the past week, including Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro (2.8T params, 104B active), Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling 2 Small (594B total, 17B active), Meituan's LongCat-2.5 (1.6T), Tencent's Hy4 (770B), LG's K-EXAONE 2.5 (750B, 31B active), Ant's Ling-3.2-flash (560B, 25B active) and Baidu's ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base (280B, 14B active).
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Seven-plus independent accounts (@Decoded08, @Techmeme, @thePandaily, @TechieUltimatum) posted about distinct MoE model launches within the same 7-day window, indicating MoE is the dominant architecture for frontier-scale releases. Claims are promotional announcements, not verified benchmarks.

findings.claim: Moonshot AI released open weights for Kimi K3.1 Pro, described as a 2.8T-parameter MoE with 104B active parameters, natively multimodal with 1M-token context; Huawei separately says Kimi K3.1 Pro LoRA training runs on 128 Ascend Atlas 950 cards.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Two accounts (@Decoded08, @TechieUltimatum) report the open-weights release and @thePandaily reports Huawei's Ascend training-support claim; all are company/account assertions.

findings.claim: Thinking Machines Lab debuted Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter MoE with 17B active parameters, image-ready with variable-effort scoring, live on Tinker (closed) with Apache-2.0 weights planned for release the following week after safety testing.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Reported by @Techmeme (citing the company) and @Decoded08; the weights release is a stated plan, not a confirmed completed event.

findings.claim: Huawei says the Kirin 9050 series' Da Vinci NPU is the first to run a 30B MoE LLM fully on-device offline, with claimed NPU performance up 140% and power draw down 66% vs. the prior generation; ModelBest separately claims its LES method runs a 35B MoE on an iPhone at 6.07x baseline (20.51 tokens/s).
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Both are vendor performance claims reported by @thePandaily, which itself flags that ModelBest's figures are the company's own. On-device MoE appears as an emerging theme across two posts.

findings.claim: Baidu open-sourced ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, a 280B sparse MoE activating 14B parameters per token, trained on 33.5T tokens, claiming 93.3 vs 89.4 MMLU over DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base on its own same-harness evaluation.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: Benchmark comparison comes from Baidu's own chart as noted by @thePandaily; vendor self-evaluation, not independently verified.

findings.claim: MoE is being applied beyond LLMs: a research paper describes MAPO (Mixture of Experts with Alternating Policy Optimization) for universal humanoid motion tracking, and Boson's Higgs Realtime Duplex is described as a 45B MoE multimodal realtime model.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Two posts from different accounts show MoE framing extending into robotics control and realtime multimodal agents; small sample, both single posts.

limitations: Only 17 posts in a 7-day window, mostly from a small set of aggregator/enthusiast accounts (@thePandaily, @Decoded08, @Techmeme); no posts from major semiconductor or infrastructure vendors in the account list mentioned MoE.
All model specs, benchmark scores and pricing are vendor or press-release claims; linked articles were not read and nothing is independently verified.
Engagement is low for most posts (0-24), so these announcements have limited observed attention even within this account set.
Coverage skews toward Chinese and open-weights model releases; absence of posts about other MoE developments reflects the fixed account list, not absence of activity.
No posts address MoE hardware/system-level implications (memory, interconnect, routing silicon) from the semiconductor accounts monitored.
x.coverage_note: Social signals only: posts from the last 7 days by the owner-approved accounts in config/x_watchlist.yaml that mention the keywords (at most 50 posts). A post is what an account says, not a verified fact; company posts are promotional by nature. Accounts not on the watchlist were not searched.

sources.title: DYNAMIC PARALLELISM FOR LANGUAGE MODEL INFERENCE [US20260350380A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Various examples relate to dynamic parallelism for language model inference. A pool of processing units is reconfigured between different parallelism modes during inference. In a first mode for attention computation, contextual memory data is distributed across processing units. After attention computation, the units are reprovisioned into a second mode with multi-dimensional parallelism, having tensor parallelism and sparse computation dimensions. The second mode enables processing tokens through neural networks in a sparse computation architecture. For dense models without mixture-of-experts, the sparse computation dimension equals one, allowing graceful degradation to tensor-parallel execution. Collective communication operations may facilitate transitions between modes while maintaining mathematical equivalence with non-distributed computation.

sources.title: MOE ARCHITECTURE-APPLIED LANGUAGE MODEL-BASED QNA SYSTEM FOR MANUFACTURING SITE [US20260339994A1]

sources.title: STAGED MIXED PARALLELISM REASONING METHOD AND SYSTEM FOR MOE SPARSE LARGE MODELS [US20260340345A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    The present disclosure provides a staged mixed parallelism reasoning method and system for an MoE sparse large model. The method includes: controlling the MoE sparse large model to execute the following steps layer by layer in a prefill stage: adding first MoE layer model parameters running based on a tensor parallelism strategy to each device while acquiring an expert number of each token of a prompt data sequence; then performing expert parallelism computation based on second MoE layer model parameters in each device running based on an expert parallelism strategy; restoring the tokens to device initial positions and releasing the second MoE layer model parameters; and sending a predicted token output by a last layer of the model to a first layer to execute reasoning in a decoding stage according to the predicted token and the first MoE layer model parameters in each device. The present disclosure can solve the problems that a parallelism strategy adopted by an existing MoE sparse large model reasoning technology has poor adaptability to the prefill stage and the decoding stage and large communication overhead.

sources.title: MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS MODEL OPTIMIZATION METHOD, APPARATUS, AND DEVICE [WO2026223201A1]
sources.abstract: Embodiments of the present invention disclose a mixture-of-experts model optimization method, apparatus, and device. In the embodiments of the present invention, the method comprises: acquiring an average number of tokens of a mixture-of-experts model, the tokens being basic units used by the mixture-of-experts model to process input data; determining N times the average number of tokens of the mixture-of-experts model, N being an integer or a decimal greater than 1; and requesting allocation of target GPU memory on the basis of N times the average number of of tokens, the target GPU memory being configured to store tokens during a forward-propagation process. In the method, when allocation of GPU memory is requested during forward propagation, the GPU memory is allocated on the basis of N times the average number of tokens, thereby solving the problem of GPU memory fragmentation, reducing the GPU memory occupied by the mixture-of-experts model, and achieving optimization of the mixture-of-experts model.

sources.title: Method and System for Agent-Based Semantic Characterization and Self-Supervised Validation of Electronic Components Using Simulation and Expert Feedback [US20260330113A1]
sources.abstract: A system and method for semantic characterization and validation of electronic components using a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agent architecture. The system comprises: (1) a content orchestration agent responsible for extraction and normalization of device datasheet information, and (2) a simulation-generation agent which produces subcircuit models using a structured grammar and validates them via self-supervised SPICE simulations. The agents collaborate iteratively to construct scenarios reflective of real-world operating conditions, bridging the gap between idealized datasheet curves and actual component behavior. Simulation results are analyzed using clustering algorithms to form a performance taxonomy, enabling deterministic classification, similarity analysis, and circuit design recommendations.

sources.title: NPU-Friendly Token Routing for Mixture-of-Experts Based Large Language Models on Edge Devices [US20260320352A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A neural processing unit (NPU) controls the routing of input tokens to experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) network. The NPU generates a routing table having a batch dimension of Bs and an expert dimension of N. Each element in the routing table is a probability value of routing an input token to an expert. The NPU further generates an expert selection vector indicating K top-ranked experts for each input token by performing quantization operations and rectified linear operations on N probability values along the expert dimension of the routing table with respect to the input token. The NPU further generates N sets of one-hot expert projection vectors for respective experts based on the routing table and expert selection vectors for the Bs input tokens. The N sets of one-hot expert project vectors are used to select the input tokens to dispatch to the experts.

sources.title: Aerial image classification system [US12762840B1]

sources.abstract: Embodiments of the present application provide a method of adjusting a model and related devices for adjusting a model. This method includes: obtaining a gating network logit value of each expert network in a first MoE layer corresponding to each token in T tokens based on the T tokens and a target MoE model; obtaining К selected expert networks corresponding to each token in the T tokens based on the logit value of each expert network in the first MoE layer corresponding to each token in the T tokens; obtaining an adjusted first MoE layer by pruning at least one expert network in the first MoE layer based on the К selected expert networks corresponding to each token in the T tokens; obtaining an adjusted target MoE model based on the adjusted first MoE layer. The proposed technique is applied for each MoE model layer in layer-by-layer manner and adjusts a MoE model to reduce a cost of resources required for deploying the MoE model.

sources.title: MODELED CONVERSIONS FOR A CONNECTION NETWORK SYSTEM [US20260278339A1]
sources.abstract: Modeled conversions for connection networking are described. A method comprises generating a first input vector comprising a set of sequence features for a group of entities using a transformer layer of a machine learning model, generating a second input vector comprising a set of identity profile features for the group of entities using a generative artificial intelligence layer, receiving a third input vector comprising a set of conversion features, concatenating the first input vector, the second input vector, and the third input vector into a concatenated vector, normalizing the concatenated vector to form a normalized vector, projecting the normalized vector to form a projected vector, and generating a first metric based on the projected vector using a multi-gate mixture-of-experts (MMOE) layer of the ML model, the first metric comprising a value indicating whether there is a deterministic entity level conversion event for a group level conversion event.

sources.title: METHOD FOR DETERMINING STRENGTH OF TREE TRUNK [US20260266791A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A method for determining strength of a tree trunk includes connecting one end of a cable to an attachment point on the tree trunk above ground, with another end of the cable being connected through a strain gauge to a winch, wherein the winch applies a pulling force through the cable to the tree trunk until a deflection of the tree trunk meets a predefined deflection threshold. The method further includes measuring, using the strain gauge and a protector, a magnitude as well as application angle of the pulling force, respectively, and using the measured magnitude as well as application angle of the pulling force, based on a pre-established model that correlates a pulling force applied to the tree trunk with a displacement of the tree trunk, calculating a Modulus of Elasticity (MoE) of the tree trunk, that represents the strength of the tree trunk.

sources.title: DATA PROCESSING METHOD AND APPARATUS [WO2026184444A1]
sources.abstract: A data processing method, comprising: performing word segmentation on an input sequence, and mapping a word segmentation result into a first vocabulary index; and processing the first vocabulary index by means of a first neural network model to obtain an inference result, wherein in a first mixture-of-experts layer of the first neural network model, on the basis of the first vocabulary index, a first lookup table stored in a memory is queried to obtain outputs of expert networks in the first mixture-of-experts layer, the first lookup table comprises the mapping relationship between indexes in a vocabulary and results obtained by performing inference on embedding representations of the indexes by the expert networks in the first mixture-of-experts layer, and the vocabulary is a word set used by the first neural network model. In the method, expert networks in mixture-of-experts layers do not need to be loaded during inference, thereby reducing video random-access memory usage and communication traffic, eliminating expert network computation in the mixture-of-experts layers, and improving inference efficiency.

sources.title: Efficient parameter multiplexing method for migrating self-supervised pre-training model to V-MoE [CN122655894A]
sources.abstract: The invention discloses an efficient parameter multiplexing method for migrating a self-supervised pre-training model to V-MoE, and belongs to the technical field of deep learning and computer vision. Constructing an input feature block sequence based on the label-free image calibration set, extracting a to-be-migrated feedforward parameter pool in the dense model, and calculating neuron activation selectivity; dividing proprietary neurons and general neurons according to activation selectivity, and respectively constructing a core expert group and a general expert group; constructing a tagged fine tuning set, calculating the local feature complexity of feature blocks, and shunting low-complexity blocks and high-complexity blocks to different expert groups; and obtaining final feature representation based on expert output, and performing downstream fine tuning on the migration model in combination with task loss and core expert load balancing loss. According to the method, differentiated multiplexing of the pre-training parameters is realized, the routing cold start risk is reduced, and dynamic computing power distribution is realized according to the local feature complexity, so that the reasoning efficiency and prediction performance of the model in a downstream visual task are improved.

sources.title: Document-level multi-event argument extraction method based on sparse mixed experts [CN122655736A]
sources.abstract: The invention belongs to the technical field of natural language processing and information extraction, and particularly relates to a document-level multi-event argument extraction method based on sparse mixed experts. Aiming at the problems of representation bottleneck and cross-event argument confusion existing when an existing dense model processes a high-density event interleaved document, the method introduces SwiGLU bilinear gating into document-level event extraction based on fine-grained MoE. In combination with condition level replacement and computing power conservation design, the model can dynamically activate specific experts according to semantics, a parameter space is multiplied on the premise that reasoning computing power is not increased, and decoupling of model capacity and computing cost and precise separation of complex semantics are perfectly achieved.

sources.title: CONTROLLING ACCESS TO INTERNAL KNOWLEDGE IN A LANGUAGE MODEL USING A MIXTURE OF EXPERTS TUNING [US20260252875A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    An approach is provided for access control management. Experts included in a mixture of experts (MoE) architecture are trained. A router selects a set of experts from the MoE model architecture as having greatest probabilities of being relevant to a data point received at the router. An expert in the set is identified as not having a privilege allowing access to the data point. A masking mechanism masks out the identified expert from the selected set of experts and identifies a previously unselected expert that has a next greatest probability of being relevant to the data point. It is determined that the identified previously unselected expert has the privilege allowing access to the data point. Based on the identified previously unselected expert having the privilege allowing the access to the data point, the identified previously unselected expert is added to the selected set of experts.

sources.title: TIME-SERIES FORECASTING FRAMEWORK WITH MOE ARCHITECTURE [US20260249873A1]

sources.abstract: An example operation includes one or more of receiving sensor data from a vehicle, determining to perform a predictive task for the vehicle, identifying temporal attributes and spatial attributes within the sensor data, determining a time-series forecasting model from among a plurality of time-series forecasting models within a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture for performing the predictive task based on at least one of the temporal attributes and the spatial attributes, executing the determined time-series forecasting model on the temporal attributes and the spatial attributes to execute the predictive task, and controlling the vehicle based on execution of the predictive task.

sources.title: TRAFFIC FORECASTING AND ROUTING BASED ON MOE ARCHITECTURE [US20260251461A1]

sources.abstract: An example operation includes one or more of receiving a current geographic location of a vehicle traveling along a travel route from at least one hardware sensor installed on the vehicle, predicting an upcoming geographic location of the vehicle based on the current geographic location of the vehicle, selecting an artificial intelligence (AI) model from among a plurality of AI models in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) based on the upcoming geographic location of the vehicle, forecasting traffic parameters at the upcoming geographic location based on execution of the selected AI model on sensor data from the upcoming geographic location, and rerouting the vehicle to a different travel route based on the forecasted traffic parameters at the upcoming geographic location.

sources.title: MULTI-PARAMETER MRI-BASED BREAST CANCER AUXILIARY DECISION-MAKING METHOD, AND RELATED APPARATUS [WO2026175015A1]
sources.abstract: Disclosed in the present invention are a multi-parameter MRI-based breast cancer auxiliary decision-making method, and a related apparatus. The method comprises: acquiring an MRI dataset, comprising MRI sequences of different modalities; performing feature extraction on multi-parameter MRI of sample data to obtain multi-modal features; using the multi-modal features and label data to perform optimization training on a preset model, so as to obtain a target model, in the preset model, a sparse mixture-of-experts being added to a preceding Transformer block, and a soft mixture-of-experts model being added to a following Transformer block; and using the target model to perform breast cancer auxiliary decision-making. The present invention can learn specific feature representations for different MRI modalities, can implement deep fusion and interactive modeling of multi-modal information, effectively improves the accuracy and robustness of models with respect to differential diagnosis of breast cancer, lays a technical foundation for non-invasive and personalized management, and can be widely used in the technical field of imaging data processing.

sources.title: Querying database systems using queries generated from natural language user input [US12717790B1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Methods, systems, and computer-readable storage media for querying database systems using queries generated by prompting of LLMs to generate query statements from natural language, where a LLM system provides a set of query statements in response to user input that is provided in natural language, the set of query statements includes a first query statement provided using an in-context prompt, a second query statement provided using a chain-of-thought (CoT) prompt, a third query statement provided using a contrastive CoT prompt, and a fourth query statement provided using a mixture-of-experts (MoE) prompt, and a query statement is selected from the set of query statements and is used to query a database system, which returns a query result responsive to the query statement.

sources.title: MOE model unloading reasoning system based on visual information-expert affinity [CN122635524A]
sources.abstract: An MOE model unloading inference system based on visual information-expert affinity comprises a visual compression module, an expert prediction module and a cache execution module, discrete expert activation caused by redundant visual tokens is reduced by conducting affinity perception compression on the visual tokens, multi-layer expert prediction and asynchronous prefetching are executed by means of a compression result, and therefore the complexity of the cache execution module is reduced. And meanwhile, a multi-dimensional cache and pipeline optimization strategy is combined, so that the reasoning speed of the visual language hybrid expert model in different video memory resource scenes is improved, and single-card reasoning acceleration under the condition that the video memory is limited is realized.

sources.title: Hardware acceleration optimization method, device and system oriented to large language model [CN122635441A]
sources.abstract: The invention provides a large language model-oriented hardware acceleration optimization method, device and system, and the method comprises the steps: constructing a GEMM and multi-GEMM parallel scheduling scheme, constructing an online Softmax calculation unit, and optimizing an attention mechanism and storage overhead through quantization and dequantization; according to the method, the multi-Token parallel computing in the pre-filling stage is realized by designing a link table-based hybrid expert MoE routing unit and designing a link table-based hybrid expert MoE routing unit, the memory wall and the cost bottleneck of large model deployment are effectively broken through, the memory bandwidth utilization rate is increased to 85% or above, efficient reasoning of a 120B parameter level MoE model can be realized on single low-cost equipment, and the decoding speed exceeds 10 token/s. The method can support the parallel distribution of multiple paths of Tokens to corresponding experts to execute MLP calculation, thoroughly improves the problem of low calculation power utilization rate of traditional serial routing, and greatly improves the batch data processing efficiency in the pre-filling stage.

findings.claim: Filing activity is accelerating rapidly, with over 300 publications in 2026 so far, and recent applications describe a shift toward infrastructure optimization and cross-domain deployment.

findings.rationale: The system reports 320 publications in 2026 year-to-date. The retrieved sample shows a clear trend: early filings focused on core model architecture, while recent applications heavily target hardware acceleration, memory management, and vertical industry integration, indicating maturation of the technology stack.

findings.claim: Hardware efficiency and memory management dominate recent filings, as applicants describe techniques to address GPU fragmentation, VRAM usage, and token routing overhead on edge and accelerator devices.

findings.rationale: Multiple independent filings target the computational bottlenecks of sparse models. Alibaba addresses GPU memory fragmentation, Huawei reduces VRAM usage via lookup tables, MediaTek optimizes routing for NPUs, and NVIDIA proposes dynamic parallelism modes. This indicates a strong industry focus on making MoE deployment feasible on constrained hardware.

findings.claim: MoE architectures are being adapted for specialized domains beyond language models, with applications describing use cases in automotive forecasting, medical imaging, manufacturing Q&A, and database querying.

This suggests the architecture is maturing and being customized for vertical industry workloads.

draft.summary: Research activity on mixture of experts (MoE) is rising very fast. OpenAlex papers went from 767 in 2024 to 2,336 in 2025, and the year-to-date count is up 239% on 2025. Patent filings are also accelerating, with 306 so far this year against 185 at the same date in 2025. The scientific findings show that MoE separates total model size from per-token compute (S2). However, the Risk challenges stress that this holds for compute only. Memory, communication and serving complexity remain, and several efficiency figures are developer-reported or cannot be attributed to MoE alone (C1, C2, C3). The same literature repeatedly reports unresolved failure modes: load imbalance, expert collapse and fragile compression (R1, R3, R5). Social posts describe a wave of very large MoE releases, but these are unverified announcements, not evidence of customer adoption or revenue (X1). The only filing-based commercial evidence is one very small, loss-making company (M1, M2). The main uncertainty is whether technical and research momentum translates into paying customers and durable economics. Research volume is not commercial success.
draft.plain_summary: Mixture of experts is a way of building very large AI models in which only a small part of the model is used for each request, which saves computing effort. Research papers, patents and new model announcements are all growing quickly, but there is little confirmed proof yet that customers are paying for it at scale. The main thing that could stop it is that the savings in computing are partly offset by memory, data-movement and reliability problems that have not been solved.

bear.label: forecast

Reported speedups prove narrow and author-run (R7). The scaling advantage is an extrapolation that does not hold at frontier scale (C3).
